system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5ad1f30514c3",
  "problem": "Which risk areas and activities embedded evaluators should prioritize given limited scope and expertise.",
  "did": "Focused on four areas tied to the Hugging Face incident that fit Transluce's expertise in model behavior evaluation, and excluded cybersecurity controls and work duplicating others.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a comprehensive list of risks",
   "improving cybersecurity controls on agent swarms",
   "duplicating METR's frontier risk reports"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They are not cybersecurity experts and want to complement rather than duplicate ongoing activities."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:836999a53f7c",
  "problem": "Testing whether future adversaries could evade the auditor, given that the evaluated attacks were not designed against it.",
  "did": "They tried distraction-based evasion attempts themselves, and discussed other possible evasions (more covert steganography, clean-label backdoors, jailbreaking the auditor) without evaluating them.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "more covert steganography",
   "clean-label backdoors",
   "semantic backdoor triggers",
   "datasets that jailbreak the auditor itself"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "An adversary may construct datasets that cannot be understood by the auditor or that distract it, so detection metrics alone do not establish robustness."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:52905219a4a4",
  "problem": "How to evaluate whether AI can cause catastrophic harm, given uncertainty about which specific cognitive capabilities are limiting.",
  "did": "They chose end-to-end, threat-model-driven task evaluations built as a chain from real-world threat to measurable proxies, rather than measuring isolated cognitive abilities.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "directly identifying the key missing cognitive capability and measuring that",
   "generic ML benchmarks",
   "academic fine-grained questions about specific reasoning"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It is hard to know the limiting capabilities, and going straight to a particular dimension risks it not being linked to the real-world outcomes of concern; benchmarks also saturate quickly and are poor proxies for models."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b641be314c14",
  "problem": "How to interpret the best agent score on the noisy Finetune GPT-2 for QA environment.",
  "did": "They reran the best agent solution, found its score dropped from 0.88 to 0.69, and concluded the original result was partly overfitting to noise, so the environment likely underestimates the human-AI gap.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The rerun score was significantly lower than the original, indicating the high score was partially driven by noise."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:5585ddf9e6f5",
  "problem": "Choosing a held-out evaluation for the decoder that tests generalization to unseen user attributes.",
  "did": "Finetuned on 78 of 80 SynthSys attributes and held out \"gender\" and \"age\" for evaluation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Evaluating on held-out attributes tests question-answering ability beyond the finetuning distribution."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:95e1b7ab2e28",
  "problem": "How to check that hacking in the chess experiment is not caused by number-sequence training degrading alignment",
  "did": "Trained two kinds of control students: one on numbers from the unsteered base model, and others on numbers from teachers steered with random vectors.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To rule out the possibility that training on number sequences causes hacking by degrading the model's alignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:d4a6567d931a",
  "problem": "How to interpret the flag rate of the LLM monitor on open-test original benchmarks, where ground truth is not known to be non-cheating.",
  "did": "They manually examined some flagged transcripts, found most were genuine cheating attempts, and so treated the flag rate only as an upper bound on the false positive rate.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Most manually examined flagged transcripts were indeed cheating, via test modification and special-casing, so the flags are not all false positives."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:68603702a152",
  "problem": "How to treat LLM unreliability (hallucination, false positives) when assessing attacker viability.",
  "did": "They argued that failures only proportionally reduce attacker value rather than preventing deployment, and that false-positive validation cost will fall as models improve.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Developing and monetizing exploits tolerates failures, since a 1% or 10% failure rate only reduces potential value by that fraction."
 }
]
